how_we_counted: The water is what Copernicus EMS outlined as flooded area or flood trace on its first map of each area (EMSR517/518/520). Later monitoring maps add water seen days afterwards; they are shown as small print, never mixed into a headline.
Residents are GHS-POP 2020 counts, each ~1 km cell weighted by the share of it under the observed water, on a 20 m equal-area grid (EPSG:3035).
Outside the 1-in-100-year zone means the 20 m cell is dry in the JRC river flood hazard map for that return period (depth 0 or no data).
Buildings are GHS-OBAT points inside the observed water; "destroyed" is the Copernicus analysts' damage grade, available only for German grading maps.
Country totals are counted on the union of the areas, cell by cell and building by building, so two maps over the same valley are not counted twice.
limits: Satellite snapshots, not the peak. Copernicus maps show the water visible on one image, often a day or more after the crest. The true extent was larger.
Outside a mapped area means not mapped, not dry. Only the outlined areas were mapped; whole flooded valleys lie outside them.

Two kinds of maps. Delineation maps, drawn semi-automatically from radar, stop at building walls and miss water between houses; grading maps, drawn by analysts, carry the water through the towns. Belgium has only delineation maps, which is why its building count is low.
Population is a model. GHS-POP 2020 (E2020) spreads residents evenly within each ~1 km cell; it does not know who was home in July 2021.

The hazard map covers large rivers only. The JRC map models rivers with catchments of 150 km² and more, without dikes, and no surface runoff or small streams: much of the 2021 damage came from exactly those.
Permanent water is excluded from the map scores (it is wet in every map and would count as a free hit); residents beside it are still counted.

Plan review date: Directive 2007/60/EC (Floods Directive), Article 14(3): flood risk management plans "shall be reviewed, and if necessary updated ... by 22 December 2021 and every six years thereafter"; the next review falls on 22 December 2027.
